note.text: The Cold War was a prolonged rivalry centred on the United States and Soviet Union, involving power, ideology, security and competing political-economic systems. Their wartime alliance against Nazi Germany did not remove earlier distrust. After 1945, disputes over Germany, Eastern Europe and reconstruction intensified suspicion. The United States feared expanding communist influence; Soviet leaders sought security and imposed influence over neighbouring states. These explanations must be assessed critically rather than accepted as complete justifications. Rivalry developed through a sequence, not one universally agreed starting incident.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to explain how the wartime alliance gave way to rivalry and distinguish ideological disagreement from postwar security disputes. Builds on: the Second World War and the changing international setting of African nationalism. Leads to: the Cold War’s policies, alliances and conflicts.

sections.heading: Explain the history
sections.text: The Cold War was a prolonged rivalry centred on the United States and Soviet Union, involving power, ideology, security and competing political-economic systems. Their wartime alliance against Nazi Germany did not remove earlier distrust. After {1945}, disputes over Germany, Eastern Europe and reconstruction intensified suspicion. The United States feared expanding communist influence; Soviet leaders sought security and imposed influence over neighbouring states. These explanations must be assessed critically rather than accepted as complete justifications. Rivalry developed through a sequence, not one universally agreed starting incident.

sections.heading: Follow the evidence and examples
sections.text: Yalta and Potsdam in {1945} concerned the postwar settlement. Differences over elections, occupation zones, reparations and influence in Eastern Europe helped undermine cooperation. Churchill’s Iron Curtain speech in {1946} expressed a Western interpretation of the division; it did not create every division by itself. American and Soviet accounts often presented their own actions as defensive and the other side’s as aggressive. Compare those claims with decisions and effects. Germany’s occupation and later division became a central arena of tension.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Distinguish a background disagreement from an action escalating it. Explain how one side’s security measure could be read as a threat by the other, while still examining coercion and responsibility. Do not describe all countries as passive objects: smaller states and anticolonial movements pursued aims of their own. Cold does not mean that no armed conflicts or deaths occurred.

cards.idea: Connect a specific action or event to the historical feature it illustrates.
example: American and Soviet leaders promoted contrasting visions of political power and economic organisation.
Disagreement over Eastern European governments intensified mistrust after {1945}.
Former allies increasingly disagreed over Germany’s future and reconstruction.
Each government describes its policy as defensive while criticising its rival’s intentions.

cards.idea: Check a claim against the sequence, setting and limits of the evidence.
example: The former allies had identical political systems and no ideological differences. Correction: Shared opposition to Nazi Germany did not eliminate their different systems or aims.
Every dispute concerned only sporting competition. Correction: Control and security in postwar Europe were central political issues.
The alliance against Hitler guaranteed permanent agreement after the war. Correction: A common enemy had supported cooperation without settling later conflicting interests.
An official’s claim that a policy is defensive proves every effect was harmless. Correction: Official claims reveal standpoint; actions, effects and other sources must also be examined.
